content: Efforts to link individuals to care and treatment following hepatitis awareness campaigns have faced challenges. In Egypt, the Egyptian Liver Research Institute in Mansoura implemented a community-based campaign in El Othmanya village to encourage household testing for hepatitis B (HBV) and C (HCV) among adolescents and adults. Approximately 22% of individuals tested were HBV DNA positive. Eligible cases were referred to the Egyptian Liver Hospital for treatment, with costs covered through community fundraising or government health insurance. This model is now being expanded to 30 additional villages. In Japan, the government has provided free hepatitis testing every five years for citizens aged 40 to 70 since 2001. In Ishikawa Prefecture, 38% of the target population (240,180 individuals) were tested. Diagnosed patients receive annual follow-ups for liver fibrosis staging and treatment. In Mongolia, where hepatitis B and C prevalence and liver cancer rates are among the highest globally, the local NGO FIRE has collaborated with primary care clinics since 2011 to conduct viral hepatitis and liver cancer screenings in rural areas. These screenings target high-risk individuals and include blood tests, ultrasounds, physical exams, counseling, and referrals. Awareness events and healthcare worker training are also part of the program. In Gambia, the PROLIFICA program is the first communityand facility-based initiative in sub-Saharan Africa to screen and treat HBV. It offers testing to all individuals aged 30 and older in rural and urban areas. Those testing positive for HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) are referred for outpatient assessment to determine treatment eligibility. In Amsterdam, the Public Health Service used an online risk assessment tool to encourage at-risk groups to evaluate their HCV risk. Participants identified as high-risk were offered anonymous HCV testing. Approximately 9,700 individuals completed the assessment, 1,500 were offered testing, and 28% utilized the testing facility. Results were accessible online, along with invitations for confirmatory testing. Workplace testing has been used to provide access to hepatitis testing for employed individuals who may face barriers to clinical services due to work commitments. However, concerns about coercion, confidentiality breaches, and weak service linkages must be addressed. For example, in the Middle East and North Africa, 60% of HIV testing occurs through mandatory workplace or visa procedures, which is not an effective model for scaling up hepatitis testing. Nonetheless, workplace testing for HIV and tuberculosis (TB) has been successfully implemented in high-burden settings. In the United States, Stanford University's Asian Liver Center partnered with 42 corporations to raise awareness about HBV and HCV testing. An online tool allowed employees to assess their hepatitis B risk and decide on testing. School-based testing programs can improve access for sexually active young people who may face challenges seeking testing during school hours. In South Africa, a national campaign offers HIV testing to students aged 12 and older. However, school-based testing remains controversial, and further evaluation is needed to address confidentiality, linkage to care, and adolescents' experiences. Prison settings present an opportunity to expand testing among high-risk populations, as many prisoners are at increased risk of hepatitis B and C. In Victoria, Australia, a state-wide program screens all prisoners for viral hepatitis upon entry or transfer. Those testing positive are referred for further assessment and antiviral therapy. The program integrates telemedicine consultations and direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) into the prison healthcare system. Decentralization of hepatitis testing services, which involves delivering services closer to patients' homes, can reduce transportation costs and waiting times, improving testing uptake. This approach has been effective in scaling up HIV services in resource-limited settings. However, centralized services may be more appropriate in some contexts, such as low-prevalence areas or for populations fearing stigma. Task-shifting, where responsibilities are transferred to trained lay providers or nurses, has been effective in addressing healthcare workforce shortages. This approach has been successfully used in HIV testing and treatment programs globally and could be adapted for hepatitis services. Peer-led interventions have also increased testing and care access for marginalized groups, such as people who inject drugs (PWID). Innovations in diagnostic technology, such as point-of-care (POC) testing, simplified algorithms, and self-testing, have the potential to expand access to hepatitis testing. POC tests, which provide results within two hours, are particularly useful in community-based settings. Multiplex tests that detect multiple infections simultaneously are also being developed. Hepatitis testing should prioritize high-risk populations, including PWID, men who have sex with men (MSM), prisoners, and sex workers. Testing must be voluntary, equitable, and provided in a supportive environment free of stigma and discrimination. Integration of hepatitis testing with other health services, such as HIV and TB care, can improve accessibility and efficiency. In summary, expanding hepatitis testing requires innovative approaches, integration with other health services, decentralization, task-shifting, and addressing barriers such as stigma and discrimination. These strategies can improve access to testing, care, and treatment for high-risk and underserved populations.
